rationale: Start with a broad, moderately fast scouting gradient to locate the elution window and critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A midrange temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity.
Use the available time margin to test a shallower gradient, targeting the crowded middle peaks. Keeping composition endpoints and temperature fixed isolates the effect of gradient slope.

Slightly reduce the gradient slope to raise the remaining critical pair toward full resolution while keeping the last peak near 10 minutes. The previous runs indicate that 0.85 organic is comfortably above the composition needed to elute all compounds.

Increase the slope slightly from 0.0536 to 0.055 organic fraction per minute, targeting a last peak just below 10 minutes while retaining R ≥ 1.5. The final composition remains above the composition at which the last peak eluted in injection 3.

Injection 4 reaches the maximum CRF; now test whether a 5 °C temperature increase shortens elution while preserving full resolution. Keeping the gradient fixed isolates the temperature response of the critical cluster.

Test whether higher temperature separates the critical pair again after an elution-order crossover suggested by its convergence at 45 °C. Keep the gradient fixed to assess this selectivity change, retaining injection 4 as the maximum-score fallback.
Shorten the gradient by one grid step to seek faster full resolution at 55 °C. Monitor both close middle pairs, keeping injection 6 as the faster maximum-score fallback.

Reduce the slope modestly relative to injection 7 to recover resolution of the new critical pair while retaining most of the time savings. This intermediate slope should place both close pairs above R = 1.5.

Shift the gradient window upward while preserving its slope to test whether initial retention can be reduced without losing full resolution. Injection 8 remains the fastest fully resolved method so far; monitor the two close middle pairs and early-peak compression.

Explore a faster, hotter gradient that may move the converging middle pair through an elution-order crossover and restore separation on the other side. This is an exploratory speed test; injection 8 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Test a higher starting organic fraction to increase separation of the crossed middle pair, combined with a shallower slope to protect its neighboring pair. This targets full resolution in the roughly five-minute elution window found in injection 10.

Explore lower-temperature selectivity with a relatively fast gradient, since the warmer fast methods trade one unresolved middle pair for another. This tests a distinct separation regime while retaining injection 8 as the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Lower the starting organic fraction to improve the pair that limited injection 7, while increasing the slope to shorten late elution. This tests whether better initial focusing can preserve full resolution in a faster gradient.

Test intermediate-temperature selectivity, where the critical cluster may separate better than at either 25 or 40 °C under a fast gradient. Injection 13 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Increase the endpoint by one grid step from injection 13 to test the speed limit of this fully resolved regime. The two close middle pairs have little margin, so this run will establish whether the steeper gradient remains acceptable.

Test whether a steeper gradient at 60 °C separates the crossed middle pair seen in injection 10, using a lower starting organic fraction to protect early and neighboring peaks. Injection 13 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-score method.

Refine between injections 7 and 8 with a slope of 0.065 organic fraction per minute, targeting full resolution near the faster boundary. This should retain slightly more critical-pair margin than injection 13 while eluting sooner than injection 8.

Test whether the lower starting organic fraction improves the critical cluster enough to permit a faster fully resolved method at 40 °C. This isolates temperature relative to injection 13 and checks an alternative selectivity regime before final refinement.

Test a higher starting composition at 40 °C, where greater initial retention than at 60 °C may protect the early pair while shifting middle-cluster selectivity. This explores a potentially faster fully resolved window, with injection 13 retained as the best confirmed speed result.

Test whether a steep gradient at 50 °C resolves the middle cluster through a different selectivity balance than at 55–60 °C. The low starting organic fraction protects early separation; injection 13 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved fallback.

Reduce the slope relative to injection 9 to recover its unresolved middle pair while retaining the higher starting composition. This targets another maximum-score method with potentially greater resolution margin than the fastest confirmed method, injection 13.

Reduce the slope slightly from injection 21 to bring its remaining critical pair above R = 1.5 while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes. This targets an additional maximum-score method; injection 13 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved choice.

Check the remaining intermediate-temperature selectivity regime using the gradient of the fastest fully resolved method. This tests whether the crowded peaks observed at 25 and 35 °C separate between those temperatures, while retaining injection 13 as the confirmed maximum-score fallback.

Test the next attainable steeper slope above injection 17, targeting the boundary where its critical pair reaches R = 1.5. The earlier final hold may delay the last peak somewhat, but injection 13 remains a confirmed maximum-score fallback.

Preserve injection 13’s successful slope and starting composition while shortening the programmed gradient to six minutes. The critical cluster should elute before the final hold; the last peak may be delayed but is expected to remain below ten minutes, retaining maximum CRF.
